115.t: First school in Tyler and the fire that burned it
115.s: He started school at five in a mixed school in a grove; it was burned down and classes moved to a Sanctified church until a new school was built.
115.ch: Childhood in Tyler, Beaumont and Houston
115.q: And so I was going there. And one night as I was coming home to my mother and my stepfather, we saw this big blaze. And we was wondering where it came from, you see. And the school had caught fire. Someone had set it on fire.

115.t: Grammar school in Houston, athletics and a Catholic school in Dallas
115.s: He finished grammar school in Houston's Fourth Ward, played ball and high-jumped, and had earlier been to a Catholic school in Dallas.
115.ch: Childhood in Tyler, Beaumont and Houston
115.q: Like that, and I was quite young then, see. So when we left Dallas and went to Houston, --

115.t: Moving to Dallas and Booker T. Washington High
115.s: The family went to Dallas where Gus attended Booker T. Washington, the only high school in North Dallas.
115.q: They had a -- my father had, before they built Washington.

115.t: Leaving Beaumont for Houston; a cousin teaches at his school
115.s: After about three years in Beaumont he and his mother moved to Houston, where he found a cousin was teaching at his grammar school.
115.ch: Childhood in Tyler, Beaumont and Houston
115.q: And -- that's right, because I was going to Gregory Grammar School in Houston, in the fourth ward. And so come to find out I had a cousin teaching at the school. I didn't know it until my mother saw him, this is it was at Chestnut.

383.s: Wilson remembers the undefeated Tuskegee football teams and the runner Benjamin Stevenson, compared locally to Red Grange.
383.q: Another thing comes to mind about Tuskegee that might be of interest to some people -- Tuskegee was quite a school sports, especially football. The baseball was not outstanding, but the Tuskegee football team went for, oh, five years undefeated. I remember one period there in the twenties, largely…

383.t: Booker T. Washington's successor Robert Moton and growing up with his children
383.s: Washington was dead before Wilson arrived; he discusses Principal Moton, the Moton children, and the quality of Tuskegee education.
383.q: No, by the time my mother and my brother and I had joined my father at Tuskegee, Booker T. Washington had died, and Robert Moten was the new principal.

383.s: Wilson and Hinton defend Washington's 22 trades as a route out of slavery's lowest labor, noting later critics wanted more liberal arts.
383.q: That's right. Booker T. Washington installed 22 trades at Tuskegee -- there was a machine shop practice, for making metal parts out of machinery; there was auto mechanics; there was printing, on up to newspaper cylinder press; work on up to job printing, on up to linotype operations, architectural…

226.t: Fair student, curriculum and which schools he attended
226.s: He was a fair student taught reading, writing and arithmetic; they sort out the order of Douglas and Drake and a memoir error.
226.q: I was a fair student. I wasn’t the greatest, but I was pretty fair on all the subjects in those days. They weren’t as separate as – separated as much. There was a curriculum of standards things that were taught to you, period. That’s what you – that’s what the class is. You didn’t move from one…

226.t: The Irish teacher and the dream of sitting behind a desk
226.s: A Willard teacher told him to aim for the post office, but he wanted to sit behind a desk in charge.
226.q: Not until I got to Willard School was there any teacher that I can recall that I remembered, and this teacher in particular – I can’t recall her name right now – was one that I remember very well. She was a big Irish woman. She was a very good teacher and nice to me. But she said to me I should not…

90.s: Barely audible remarks about the Piney Woods school and another piano player.
90.q: ...one of the most beautiful things I ever saw. ...(?)... It was like ....(?)....(?)....(?)....(?)....(?)....(?).... people of all races, all nationalities, everybody ...(?)... ....(?)....(?).... to do their thing. It was really wild, you know.

90.t: Jackson State, Cameron College and Jim Hill school
90.s: Names of Jackson's Black schools and colleges and the Reconstruction figures they were named for.
90.q: I don't know the name of the college. It's a ....(?). .... college. But it's the only Black college in Meridian, or they only have one... They used to have two in Jackson. There was Cameron College and Jackson College. But when the state took over Jackson and made it Jackson

712.t: Scrapbook: 1906 high school graduation and her father
712.s: Scrapbook items from her high school graduation, where she sang, and photos of her towboat-captain father.
712.q: Now, I have in here, uh, a few of the, um, uh, uh, I'll go easy. See this? Yeah. This is, uh, printed up there myself when I first got this scrapbook, of course, many years of the year. And, and this is my first, this is where, when I graduated from high school, I was a singer in those days. So,…

650.t: Fifth School, its teachers and vocal music lessons
650.s: He describes Fifth School, principal A.P. Williams, teachers Mrs. Lewis and others, and singing lessons; he left at fifteen for Southern University.
650.q: I left fifth school at the County Franklin and Padilla, fifteen years of age. I left there to go to what you call Southern University. I'd be on Southern University Magazine. You know what I said about that? It's down in Baton Rouge. But it was then on Southern University Magazine.

88.t: Father's Tuskegee education and black colleges in Louisiana
88.s: Lee says his father graduated from Tuskegee and relates how Grambling was founded with Booker T. Washington's help.
88.q: I don't really know, but I was thinking, I don't really think so because, like, I was reading the Times this morning and on the Sports page they were talking about Grambling University -- you know, that's quite a football force, in the black colleges.

232.t: Registering at Tuskegee and the Oklahoma reputation
232.s: At the registrar's office he is warned about his Oklahoma predecessors, including his brother Clarence Fields and Jake Simmons, and meets some careless Oklahoma natives.
232.q: So we went on for a little longer and that next fall I did go to Tuskegee, and so after I enrolled I was in the Registrar's office and one of the members--I forget what capacity he was in--but was Wilson, the father of Teddy Wilson, was in this office when I was registering myself, and of course…

413.t: Size, Catholic military school and school grades
413.s: At 6'4" he was embarrassed by his height; military school fixed his posture. He excelled in subjects he liked and failed gym until he joined football.
413.q: Well, I'm 6'4" now. In the 8th grade I was 6' and my feet were size 12. It was very embarrassing. I felt awkward. But I went to a Catholic military school in the 9th grade and they made me stand up straight and march and everything. So I didn't get a stoop or anything.

7.t: Going away to high school in Topeka and falling for math
7.s: He persuades his mother to send him to a school in Topeka, where good teachers make algebra and geometry click and he takes four years of math.
7.q: So when I went... I don't remember too much of the math I had in the seventh and eighth grades in Muskogee. So I talked my mother into letting me go off to school. A buddy of mine had gone to Wilberforce, came back and told me how good it was going off to school. So I found out about this school in…

125.t: School woodwork, sheet metal and auto classes
125.s: He took shop classes and made a wooden sailboat and lamps that his stepmother kept; he still enjoys woodwork.
125.q: I also took up in school, which I think is quite important, and it's a wonderful thing for people in school, is that in the schools they had these classes in woodwork, sheet metal, and auto mechanics.
